findings.title: Type-level proof is absent — types are the first API and the current proof machinery cannot see them
findings.body: The contract says 'precise types' and 'TypeScript proves types', but tsc only proves the atom compiles — nothing proves what CONSUMERS infer. For packages/core/type-helpers the entire product is type-level, and the bar's whole proof arsenal (unit tests, mutation testing, packed smoke) is nearly vacuous against it: you can break a conditional type so every consumer infers `unknown` and stay green on every mandated check. Instrument: per-atom type tests using vitest's expectTypeOf/assertType for positive inference claims, plus @ts-expect-error negative fixtures type-checked by tsc in the conformance instrument; the extension-1 negative examples that claim 'compile error' get a matching fixture so the claim is recomputed, not asserted. This is a genuine hole, not bloat: it is the only proof class in the hunt list that covers behaviour no existing bar element can even observe.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Agents consume atoms through inference at edit time; proven inference means downstream code type-checks first try instead of each consumer paying a debugging round for a silently widened type.

findings.title: TSDoc example pairs can rot — extension 1 mandates examples but nothing makes them compile or run
findings.body: Extension 1 requires ≥2 positive + ≥2 negative examples per public symbol, and the sketched conformance instrument checks example-pair COVERAGE (presence), not TRUTH. A rotted positive example is worse than none for this estate's primarily-AI workforce: agents read TSDoc at the moment of use and will faithfully reproduce a stale call shape. Instrument: the conformance validator extracts fenced ts blocks from TSDoc into generated spec files — positives must compile and (where runtime) execute; negatives must fail exactly as documented (@ts-expect-error for compile-error class, executed assertion on the named Result error for runtime class). This amends extension 1 from 'examples exist' to 'examples are recomputed structure', which is the estate's own standard — it trusts recomputed structure, never convention.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Docs that provably match the code let agents build on an atom from its TSDoc alone, in one token-cheap read, with zero risk of learning a misuse from the documentation meant to prevent it.

findings.title: Machine-independence is claimed, never executed — no cross-platform proof leg
findings.body: The contract requires 'provider-neutral, machine-independent behaviour' but the behavioural-proof section never runs anything on a second OS — the claim is convention. Windows path semantics bit this estate hard this very week, and safe-path exists precisely because of that class. Instrument: the register flags platform-sensitive atoms (paths, fs, line endings, locale/ICU, timezone); flagged atoms get a windows-latest CI matrix leg running the full unit+packed-smoke suite (cheap: atoms are small and pure), and where feasible property tests over both path styles. Unflagged pure atoms skip the matrix — conditional, so no across-the-board CI tax.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Contributors and agents on any machine can trust an atom without re-deriving its platform behaviour — the exact multiplication of cost (n consumers × per-OS debugging) the programme exists to delete, and this week's Windows lesson priced.

findings.title: Zero-runtime-dependency default — 'minimal dependencies' is not recomputed
findings.body: The contract's 'minimal external dependencies' is a judgment, not a check, yet the atom tier is where a compromised or drifting dependency has maximum fan-out: whatever an atom depends on, the whole estate transitively ships. Estate fact: today's core members can and mostly should hold ZERO runtime dependencies. Instrument: each register row declares a runtime-dependency budget (default: empty dependencies field); the conformance instrument fails on any runtime dependency not named in the row, so adding one is a visible register diff routed through review, never a silent package.json edit. Knip/depcruise already police usage and direction; this adds the missing existence check at the highest-leverage tier.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Dependency-free atoms never force estate-wide advisory response, forced bumps, or supply-chain triage — whole classes of future interruption cost go to zero at the tier with the biggest blast radius.

findings.title: API surface drift needs a committed, diffed report — extension 3 checks minimality, not change visibility
findings.body: Extension 3's validator fails on incidental exports at a point in time, but an INTENTIONAL-looking widening or signature change sails through — the surface can evolve without anyone seeing the evolution as an event. Instrument: a committed per-atom API report (api-extractor .api.md, or a rolled-up d.ts snapshot the conformance instrument recomputes and diffs) so any public-surface change is a red diff in the PR, reviewable as a contract decision. This also gives agents a single token-cheap file that IS the whole public contract. Amends extension 3 rather than adding a new element; the instrument choice should be verified against current vendor docs at tranche one, per the plan's own benchmark-harness clause.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: A one-file recomputed contract makes every API change deliberate and every atom readable by an agent in one small read — cheaper reviews now, no accidental compatibility surface to unwind later.

findings.title: Diagnostic quality of failures is aspiration ('actionable failures'), not a tested contract
findings.body: The bar preserves causes and requires README error meaning, but no instrument holds the diagnostics themselves: error codes/names and cause chains are not asserted by the mandated negative-path tests, so a message can drift to uselessness while everything stays green — and mutation testing typically ignores string literals. Instrument: modest amendment to the behavioural-proof section — each documented failure state's test asserts the discriminant (error name/code) and cause-chain presence, making the diagnostic part of the public contract the mutation policy and tests actually guard. Deliberately NOT full message-text snapshotting (that would couple tests to prose and become bloat); the discriminant and cause are the load-bearing part an agent branches on.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: An agent hitting a failure with a stable, documented discriminant self-corrects in one turn instead of a debugging excursion — multiplied by every future consumer of every atom.

findings.title: Adversarial proof for guarantee-class atoms — security posture at atom boundaries is implicit
findings.body: Some atoms' contracts ARE safety guarantees (safe-path's traversal resistance; env's validated boundary). The bar's 'validated boundaries' and example-based tests prove the happy negative cases someone thought of; a guarantee is only worth consumers DROPPING their own defensive checks if its negative space is searched adversarially. Instrument: the register flags guarantee-class atoms; flagged atoms require property tests with adversarial generators (fast-check, already consistent with the bar's property-test clause) over the attack grammar the guarantee names — e.g. encoded traversal sequences, mixed separators, unicode normalisation for safe-path. Conditional, not universal: fuzzing result or type-helpers would be pure ceremony.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Consumers can delete their own defensive re-checks only when the atom's guarantee is adversarially proven — that deletion is exactly the consumer-thinning the programme's value chain promises.

findings.title: Versioning, changelog, and deprecation discipline — not load-bearing until first external publish
findings.body: All core members are private workspace packages (0.0.0-development, no changesets), consumed atomically in-repo; house doctrine (no compatibility surface, replace-dont-bridge, validate-full-target-estate) already means a breaking change migrates every consumer in the same PR series and git history is the changelog. Adding semver/changesets/deprecation ceremony now would tax every atom for consumers that do not exist. One sentence belongs in the programme node, not the bar: first external publication of any atom mints the versioning-and-changelog discipline as a gate for the published set (the estate's open-source-public standard and MIT licensing make this plausible later).
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Withholding the ceremony keeps every atomic in-repo breaking change one cheap PR series instead of a version-dance; the recorded trigger prevents a scramble at first publish.

findings.title: Inter-atom composition law suites — covered enough within atoms; pairwise suites would be bar-bloat
findings.body: The bar already requires property/generative tests where a contract has algebraic laws, which covers the real cases (result's map/flatMap combinator laws are laws OF result's own contract). A mandatory cross-atom composition suite scales O(n²) with the register and would mostly restate what real consumers plus the contract's integration-test clause already exercise. No amendment; if a specific pair develops a genuinely shared law (e.g. graph-core operations over Result), it is a property test in whichever atom owns the law, under the existing clause.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Not adding it keeps per-atom cost flat as the register grows — a bar whose cost scales quadratically would itself slow the innovation it funds.

findings.title: Memory/allocation behaviour — the relative perf fence already catches what matters here
findings.body: For Node/TS atoms of this size, gross allocation regressions surface as time regressions inside extension 2's relative fences; a dedicated per-atom allocation budget (heap snapshots, GC pressure harnesses) is heavy instrumentation with no current atom whose CONTRACT is about memory. Revisit only if a streaming or large-buffer atom (e.g. a future image-mathematics slice over big arrays) joins the register — then the budget belongs in that atom's row, not the universal bar.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Skipping universal allocation harnesses keeps the tranche-one conformance instrument buildable and the per-atom cost proportionate; the fence still catches regressions that would actually slow consumers.

findings.title: Discoverability catalogue — mostly covered by register + conformance; make bidirectional completeness explicit
findings.body: The plan's committed atom register plus the discoverability gate covers the catalogue need, and the success criterion already implies every packages/core/* member holds a row. One cheap tightening worth folding into the tranche-one conformance instrument rather than the bar prose: recompute register↔filesystem completeness in both directions (a row naming a missing package fails; a core package missing a row fails), so the catalogue agents consult can never silently diverge from the packages that exist. This is an instrument detail for the delivery plan, not a new bar element.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: A register that provably matches the estate lets an agent answer 'does an atom for X already exist?' from one file, preventing the duplicate reimplementation the whole programme is priced against.

findings.title: Rust doctest discipline: examples must execute, or the example quota is a doc-rot generator
findings.body: Rust std's defining discipline is not 'many examples' — it is that every example is a doctest: extracted, compiled, and run on every CI pass, importing the crate as a consumer would. The candidate bar counts example PAIRS (conformance fails on a symbol missing its 2+2) but never runs them; that is exactly the failure mode Rust fenced — prose examples silently drift from the API and become confidently-wrong documentation. For an AI-agent workforce this is worse than for humans: agents apply TSDoc verbatim at edit time, so a rotted example is an injected bug, not a stale hint. Instrument for this estate: a doc-example extractor in the tranche-one conformance instrument (agent-tools already hosts the validator culture) that pulls fenced TS from every @example block into generated vitest specs, importing from the package name `@oaknational/<atom>` (workspace resolution to dist) so examples also prove the built surface — merging with the existing packed-smoke element. Negative examples get the Rust `compile_fail` treatment: a compile-error negative carries `// @ts-expect-error`, so if the misuse ever stops being an error the suite fails — every negative example doubles as an API-strictness regression test, for free. A Result-error negative asserts the actual Err value. The conformance instrument then counts only EXECUTED examples; an unexecuted example is a missing example.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Executed examples are the only docs an agent can trust without re-verifying against source, which is precisely what makes an agent's next edit cheap; rotted examples make every future edit slower than having no docs at all.

findings.title: Committed public-API report per atom (cargo-public-api / api-extractor lineage)
findings.body: The bar's 'validated strict API surface' names the goal but not the proven instrument. The mature discipline (Rust's cargo-public-api, .NET API baselines, api-extractor's .api.md) is a COMMITTED, diffable public-surface artifact per package: every export, signature, and type parameter rolled up into one reviewed file, with CI failing on drift between the built d.ts and the committed report. This gives three things the current 'fail on incidental exports' phrasing doesn't: (1) contract changes are visible in the PR diff as contract changes, so reviewers and the pre-execution code-expert see the API move, not just the implementation; (2) SemVer verdicts become recomputable (surface diff = the MAJOR/MINOR evidence), which the estate already treats as a wire-field concern; (3) incidental-export detection falls out as a side effect. Instrument: api-extractor per atom (rollup report committed, `--verify` in the conformance run), or if its ESM ergonomics chafe, a ts-morph-generated surface snapshot vitest-asserted — either satisfies the recompute-don't-record rule. Pair with `@arethetypeswrong/cli` + `publint` inside the existing packed-smoke element to prove the types actually resolve from the packed form.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: A diffable contract makes atom evolution cheap to review and safe to consume: downstream agents can read one file to know the whole surface, and breaking-change detection is mechanical rather than archaeological.

findings.title: Lodash fence: structural ban on grab-bag atoms
findings.body: Lodash's failure was not bad functions; it was that 'utility library' is a responsibility that never says no, so the surface grew to ~300 exports no one could audit, deprecate, or tree-shake confidently. The bar's 'one precisely named responsibility' is doctrine, and this estate only trusts recomputed structure. Two cheap recomputable fences: (1) a repo validator (join the existing `repo-validators:check` chain in agent-tools) that fails any `packages/core/*` member named from the grab-bag lexicon — utils, helpers, shared, common, misc, lib — names which are empirically the door grab-bags walk through; note `type-helpers` already sits on this line and deserves a register row scrutinising whether it is one responsibility or a nascent drawer. (2) knip per atom in production mode with zero tolerated unused exports, wired into the conformance instrument — an export no consumer imports is grab-bag accretion in progress, and knip already exists in this estate so the marginal cost is configuration, not new machinery.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: A single-responsibility atom is findable and wholly readable inside one agent context window; a grab-bag core makes every future 'where does this live / what does this do' question expensive forever.

findings.title: Orphaned-utility fence: consumer count is recomputed standing, not just at promotion
findings.body: fp-ts's end-state and every dead corner of lodash teach the same lesson: libraries don't announce their own obsolescence — consumers just leave, and the maintenance/assurance burden keeps running on zero fan-out. The frame's multiple-real-consumers gate fires once, at promotion; nothing in the candidate bar re-checks it. Instrument: the conformance instrument recomputes each at-bar atom's independent production consumer count on every run, via depcruise reachability from production packages (the graph machinery and `tsconfig.depcruise.json` already exist). An atom falling below two production consumers flips its register row to a demote/inline disposition — which also makes the frame's 'explicit removal condition' something the estate actually evaluates rather than a prose promise. This is the same recompute-don't-record principle the estate already applies to claims and plan gates, extended to the register's own admission evidence.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Every orphaned atom silently taxes future work — CI minutes, mutation runs, doc maintenance, agent context spent learning an atom nobody composes; automatic demotion keeps the core's total assurance burden proportional to actual leverage.

findings.title: Node stdlib deprecation lifecycle: make the removal condition executable
findings.body: Node's core is the best prior art for REMOVING things from a widely-consumed surface without breakage: a numbered deprecation ladder (doc-only → runtime-flagged → end-of-life), each stage mechanically visible to consumers, spread across majors. The bar requires an 'explicit losing or removal condition' but gives it no mechanism, which in practice means nothing is ever removed (lodash) or removal is a flag-day trauma. Estate-shaped ladder: (1) removal condition met → symbol gains `@deprecated` TSDoc with the migration target named in the message; (2) typescript-eslint's `no-deprecated` rule — the estate already owns `@oaknational/eslint-plugin-standards`, so enabling it estate-wide is one rule addition — makes every consuming site a visible lint signal, giving agents an actionable worklist instead of prose; (3) the register row tracks state (deprecated-since, consumers-remaining via the depcruise recompute above) and the atom deletes only at zero consumers. Cheap, fully recomputed, and it reuses two instruments the estate already trusts.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Replaceability is what keeps a core from ossifying: when a better atom design appears, a mechanical migration ladder makes adopting it a lint-driven sweep instead of a research project, so the estate can keep improving its foundations cheaply.

findings.title: Go benchstat discipline: perf fences must be variance-aware and same-run, or they will be disabled
findings.body: The relative-regression-fence choice is right (Go's proverb-level wisdom: measure, don't guess), but the practitioner failure mode is precise: benchmark numbers on shared CI runners vary 10-30% run-to-run, so a naive 'fail if >X% slower than the stored baseline' fence fires on noise, agents burn context chasing phantom regressions, and under this estate's no-warning-toleration rule the fence gets deleted — worse than never having it. Go solved this with benchstat: multiple samples, statistical significance before a delta is believed. Estate shape: benchmarks in vitest `bench` mode (verify against current vitest docs at tranche one, per the plan's own note); comparison is A/B WITHIN one CI job — run the baseline ref and the candidate ref on the same runner in the same job — never against a stored absolute number from a different machine; require N iterations and a significance threshold before declaring breach. Budgets recorded in the register are then honest relative fences. Second half of the discipline: a perf budget is only owed where the atom's contract makes a perf claim (a hot-path graph algorithm yes, an env parser no) — the register row should carry a declared perf-relevance so the conformance instrument knows which atoms owe benches, keeping the fence from becoming ceremony on cold-path atoms.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: A trustworthy perf fence catches a regression at the one-function layer where it is a cheap fix; a noisy fence trains everyone to ignore red, which is slower than no fence because it also erodes trust in the neighbouring gates.

findings.title: Per-symbol 2+2 example quota risks filler; Rust's actual discipline is coverage-with-judgment, executed
findings.body: Rust std does not impose a fixed example quota per item; it enforces `missing_docs` (everything documented) and runs every example that exists, with examples concentrated where misuse lives. A hard ≥2-positive+≥2-negative per PUBLIC SYMBOL will generate filler on trivial symbols (what are two honest negative examples for `isOk`?), and filler is not free here: agents read TSDoc in token-priced context windows, so padded examples tax every future edit of every consumer — a direct charge against the ultimate goal. The owner's verbatim directive says 'each one [module] with extensive TSDoc, including multiple positive and negative examples' — the per-SYMBOL quota is the plan node's extension, so amending it stays inside the directive. Proposed shape: 2+2 executed examples owed per atom ENTRY-POINT concept and per symbol with a known misuse class; other public symbols owe ≥1 executed example; any waiver is an explicit per-symbol register annotation naming why (e.g. 'trivial predicate, misuse class none'), so the conformance instrument still recomputes coverage and nothing is silently exempt. Negative examples remain mandatory wherever a misuse class exists — that is the genuinely novel, agent-leveraged part of the owner's directive and worth keeping sharp rather than diluted across filler.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Docs sized to real misuse classes maximise signal per token for the agent workforce; a mechanical quota optimises a count while slowing the readers the docs exist to speed up.

findings.title: fp-ts abstraction tax: the existing gates already fence it — add nothing
findings.body: fp-ts's arc (HKT emulation, typeclass hierarchies, ultimately folded into Effect) is the canonical abstraction-astronautics warning: abstractions that tax every consumer with encoding overhead lose to concrete, boring contracts. Checked against this estate: the promotion test's compositional-simplicity gate ('consumers become thinner'), low-context-specificity gate, and the frame's explicit discard of speculative optionality already carry this lesson, and 'abstraction tax' has no honest recomputable metric — any structural proxy (type-parameter counts, generic-depth limits) would be a lookalike measure inviting gaming or false alarms. The one estate-specific watchpoint: `packages/core/type-helpers` is the natural landing zone for astronautics; its register row (every existing member gets one, not grandfathered) is the right place for that scrutiny, and the register mechanism already exists in the plan. No bar change warranted; recording so the lesson isn't re-litigated.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Declining to add an unenforceable element keeps the bar itself cheap — every ceremony element taxes every atom forever, which is the same currency the programme is trying to save.

findings.title: Go small-API and copying proverbs: already embodied — no bar change
findings.body: Go std's disciplines — small orthogonal surfaces, 'a little copying is better than a little dependency', internal packages hiding non-contract code — map onto elements the frame already holds: the small-total-API clause, the two-consumer promotion gate (which IS the copying proverb, operationalised), and the single-entry exports map already present in `packages/core/result/package.json` (`"."` only, blocking deep imports structurally). The only import worth carrying is downstream of other findings: keeping the exports map single-entry should be asserted by the conformance instrument rather than assumed, which the committed API report (finding 2) covers as a side effect. Recorded so the survey doesn't re-derive these as gaps.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Confirming existing coverage prevents duplicate bar elements — two elements proving one claim is assurance-burden inflation with zero added speed.

findings.title: Examples must be executable, or they become misuse generators
findings.body: Agents copy @example blocks verbatim at very high rates — an example is not documentation to us, it is a template we instantiate. A stale or wrong example in an atom with high fan-out is therefore a misuse GENERATOR at the exact tier where the frame says defects have maximal blast radius. The bar's TSDoc example-pair requirement (extension 1) currently checks presence, not truth. Amend it: every @example fence is extracted and recomputed by the conformance instrument — runtime examples compiled and executed under vitest with their stated output/Result asserted; compile-error negative examples written with @ts-expect-error markers so the extractor proves they fail to compile (and fails the build if they start compiling, i.e. the misuse became silently legal). Instrument: a doc-example extractor in the conformance validator (tranche-one work, alongside the planned example-pair coverage check), running in the same CI lane as tests. This is the difference between 'examples exist' and 'examples are true', and only the second is worth tokens.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: A recomputed example can never rot, so every future agent instantiates correct use on the first try instead of shipping a copied defect that costs a review-and-rework loop multiplied by atom fan-out.

findings.title: Negative examples should graduate into a misuse register with an enforcement column
findings.body: The cheapest atom for me to use safely is one I never have to read: the type system rejects the wrong call. The owner's negative examples enumerate misuse classes — that enumeration is exactly the input needed to CLOSE those classes structurally. Add to the bar: each atom carries a misuse register (a section of its register row or package manifest) where every named misuse is classified as (a) closed-by-types — proven by a type-level test (*.test-d.ts with @ts-expect-error) showing it is uncompilable; (b) closed-by-lint — an @oaknational/oak-eslint rule ID (the plugin and rules/ directory already exist); or (c) doc-only residue — a named, counted exception. The conformance instrument recomputes that every row links to a passing type test or an enabled lint rule. Example from the live estate: safe-path returning a branded CanonicalPath instead of string would make 'passed an unvalidated path to a sink' uncompilable rather than a prose warning. The ratified contract's 'Strict total contract' gate gains a falsifiable sub-check instead of relying on reviewer vigilance.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Every misuse class moved from doc-only to uncompilable is a class of future bug, review comment, and context-window read that no agent ever pays for again — zero-read safety is the strongest possible token economy.

findings.title: Extension 3 (validated strict API) needs its instrument named: single-file API report with drift gating
findings.body: The sketch says the conformance instrument 'fails on incidental exports' but names no mechanism. The right instrument is an API report in the api-extractor mould: a rolled-up declaration file plus a committed, diffable .api.md-style report per atom, with CI failing on forgotten exports and on any surface change that is not an explicitly reviewed diff. This serves me doubly: (1) the entire public contract of an atom becomes ONE greppable file I can Read in a single call — today reading @oaknational/result's contract means walking index.ts → result-type.ts → unwrapping.ts; (2) surface growth becomes a reviewed diff, which is a relative regression fence on API sprawl exactly parallel to the perf budgets — the API surface gets the same 'no silent growth' discipline as latency. Instrument: @microsoft/api-extractor (or equivalent recomputed report) wired into the conformance validator; verify harness choice against current vendor docs at tranche-one authoring per the plan's own rule.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: A one-file, drift-gated contract collapses my tokens-to-correct-use to a single Read and makes accidental API growth — the main way atoms get expensive to change — visible at the PR where it happens.

findings.title: Typed error discriminants; message text is presentation, never contract
findings.body: Add to the bar's contract-and-boundaries section: the E in every public Result<T, E> is a discriminated union with a stable code/kind discriminant, and each arm's TSDoc states what was violated, what will be observed, and the corrective action; free-text message content is explicitly non-contractual. Agents branch on errors constantly — if the only discriminant is prose, we match on message substrings, which welds consumers to wording and makes every message improvement a breaking change (and message-matching is exactly the fragile behaviour the estate's verify-dont-trust culture exists to kill). safe-path's current throw carries an excellent message (candidate, resolution, base — the fix is in the error) but as an untyped Error it is both off-doctrine (use-result-pattern rule) and unmatchable except by string. Instrument: a type-level test per atom asserting E's union shape, plus unit tests asserting each arm carries its observed-value fields; the conformance instrument checks every public Result-returning symbol documents its E arms. Mutation testing (already mandatory) then audits that each arm is genuinely reachable.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Stable error codes let an agent go from failure to fix in one branch and one read, and let messages improve forever without a coordinated consumer migration.

findings.title: Packed-form proof should include resolution proof: publint + arethetypeswrong in the conformance lane
findings.body: The ratified contract requires a built/packed smoke proof; make part of it recomputed and cheap by adding publint and @arethetypeswrong/cli to the conformance instrument for every atom. These verify the exports map, types resolution under node16/bundler/CJS-interop conditions, and file inclusion — the class of defect that is invisible in-repo (where TypeScript project references paper over everything) and only detonates at the consumer. This week's Windows path-semantics pain is the live warrant: cross-platform and cross-resolver correctness of the shipped artefact is exactly what agents cannot see from source reading, so it must be structure. These tools are static and fast; they complement, not replace, the executing smoke proof.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Every 'works in the monorepo, breaks for the consumer' incident is a multi-agent debugging session at integration distance — the most expensive place to find a defect that a two-second static check catches at the atom.

findings.title: The per-symbol 2+2 example floor taxes every future read; scope it to behavioural symbols
findings.body: HARM flag on extension 1 as written. 'Every public symbol' includes trivial type arms — Ok<T>, Err<E>, an options interface's readonly members. Four examples on each of those turns a 30-line module into a 200-line read, and I pay that inflation on EVERY Read of the file, forever, whether or not I needed the examples — docs are free at rest but priced per-retrieval in a token-metered workforce. Worse, uniform example-noise trains agents to skim docs, eroding the value of the examples that matter. Amend: the ≥2 positive / ≥2 negative floor applies to exported behavioural symbols (functions, methods, classes); type-only symbols whose misuse is already uncompilable require a one-sentence contract summary, with their misuse classes discharged in the misuse register instead. Additionally enforce summary-first TSDoc ordering (summary line → params/returns → @remarks → @example last) so a partial read yields the contract before the elaboration; instrument: eslint-plugin-jsdoc structure rules alongside the already-installed eslint-plugin-tsdoc, plus the conformance instrument's coverage check keyed to symbol kind.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Right-sized docs keep the marginal cost of consulting an atom near zero for every future agent task, which is precisely the marginal-innovation-cost the owner is buying; uniform bloat silently raises it estate-wide.

findings.title: README must not restate the API — one retrieval surface per fact
findings.body: The ratified contract's 'progressive README covering ... API, examples' creates a second copy of the contract in prose. Two surfaces means either I read both (double tokens) or I read one and risk it being the stale one; drift between them is undetectable by any current instrument. Amend the documentation element: the README owns what TSDoc cannot carry — purpose, placement/boundaries, troubleshooting narrative, removal condition — and POINTS to the API report and TSDoc for signatures and examples, never restates them. This matches the estate's existing no-moving-targets-in-permanent-docs and documentation-hygiene doctrine applied at package scale. Instrument: primarily the doc-review lens at PR time, plus a cheap conformance check that README code fences containing atom import specifiers also appear in extracted (executed) examples — partial enforcement, honestly labelled.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: One authoritative surface per fact halves retrieval cost and eliminates the stale-copy failure mode, so future agents act on the contract, not on an unrefreshed paraphrase of it.

findings.title: Result must-use enforcement: an ignored Result is a swallowed failure
findings.body: The house Result doctrine has a structural hole the type system does not close: calling a Result-returning function as an expression statement and discarding the value compiles cleanly and silently swallows the failure — the exact outcome Result exists to prevent, and a misuse class that will otherwise appear in every atom's negative examples individually. Close it once, estate-wide: a custom rule in @oaknational/eslint-plugin-standards (the plugin and rules/ directory already exist, so this is an addition to a live instrument, not new machinery) flagging any discarded Result-typed expression, with type-aware linting. This is the single highest-leverage misuse-resistance purchase available: one rule, every atom and every consumer inherits it, no reading required.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Swallowed-error bugs are the most expensive kind to find (they present as distant mysterious state, not as a failure at the call site); making them unlintable converts a recurring multi-session debugging cost into a compile-time redline.

findings.title: The atom register doubles as the agent discovery index
findings.body: My first question is never 'how do I use this atom' but 'does an atom for this exist, and what is it called' — today that is a packages/core crawl plus grep guesses. The planned register already exists in the sketch; amend its row schema so one Read answers discovery: each row carries the exact import specifier, a one-line contract sentence, and the misuse-register pointer. The conformance instrument recomputes the register↔filesystem bijection (every packages/core member has a row; every row's specifier resolves in the packed form). At register admission, review naming against a small house vocabulary table — one verb per operation class (parse vs from vs decode never coexist as synonyms) — so names are predictable enough to grep for before the register is even consulted. The vocabulary check is reviewer-applied at admission (a judgment call, honestly not recomputable); the bijection and specifier checks are recomputed.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Discovery is the gate on all reuse — an atom an agent cannot find in one read is re-implemented, and every re-implementation resurrects the exact duplicated-responsibility cost the whole programme exists to remove.

findings.title: Benchmarks and their fixtures stay out of the source read path
findings.body: Minor placement note: perf suites tend to accumulate large fixture literals and harness code. Keep benches in a bench/ directory excluded from src/, so an agent Reading an atom's implementation or contract never pays for fixture tokens. The relative-regression-fence design in the sketch is itself sound for agent economics — no flag; absolute budgets would have been the hazard (machine-dependent flakes that train agents to ignore red). No bar change warranted; a per-tranche layout convention the first exemplar sets.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Keeps the cost of consulting an atom flat as its assurance grows, but it is layout hygiene rather than a bar element — the bar should stay small.

findings.title: Mandatory mutation testing: enforce run-freshness and survivor disposition, key the mandate to mutant population, never to score
findings.body: The estate's only data point is the type-helpers canary: 18 mutants, 18 killed, 0 survivors (packages/core/type-helpers/mutation-evidence/report.json) — bought with a dedicated plan, a mechanics report of sandbox/config archaeology, and four logged runs. At small or type-level atoms the cost is dominated by harness mechanics, not proof, and Stryker cannot mutate the type-level behaviour that IS such an atom's contract. The bar also collides with ratified doctrine: the canary config states 'Mutation score is evidence, never a gate (owner doctrine)' while the frame says 'mandatory'. Amend: the conformance instrument recomputes two facts per atom — (a) a mutation report exists newer than the atom's last source change (report.json vs git log), (b) survivor-dispositions.md dispositions every survivor in the current report — and no score threshold ever gates. Proportionality key: mutable runtime surface. Atoms whose contract is type-level (type-helpers, most of graph-core/vocab) discharge behavioural proof via compile-time assertion suites (expect-type + @ts-expect-error under tsc), which mutation testing cannot audit anyway; the mutation mandate binds only where a runtime mutant population exists to audit.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Survivor-level disposition on runtime-bearing atoms keeps the fan-out tier's tests honest where defects actually multiply, while exempting type-only atoms removes a standing harness tax that yields zero mutants.

findings.title: ≥2 positive + ≥2 negative examples per public symbol: replace fixed count with a symbol-kind × misuse-class proportional rule
findings.body: Real surface counts: graph-core 74 public symbols (≥296 examples under the rule), observability 47, env 27. Many symbols are vocabulary constants (skos.prefLabel) and type re-exports with no meaningful misuse — a fixed quota forces synthetic negatives, and the primary reader is an agent paying tokens for that filler at every edit-time doc read; the rule taxes exactly the audience it serves. Amend: proportionality key = symbol kind × enumerated misuse classes. Callable and contract-bearing symbols carry ≥1 positive example plus one negative example per NAMED misuse class (the TSDoc names the class: wrong-order args, unchecked Result, path-separator assumption); pure type re-exports and vocab constants carry one module-level positive usage. Instrument: the conformance validator walks the built export surface with ts-morph, classifies each symbol's kind, and enforces the keyed rule — falsifiable structure, no convention.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Misuse-class-keyed negatives close real agent failure modes at the moment of use while keeping every atom's doc payload proportional to its hazard, so edit-time context windows carry signal, not quota-filler.

findings.title: Add: every TSDoc example is machine-executed — examples are proof, not prose
findings.body: Nothing in the candidate bar makes examples TRUE. For an agent workforce that composes atoms by copying examples verbatim, a drifted example is worse than a missing one: it injects a defect at every reuse site. Instrument: the conformance instrument extracts ts-fenced example blocks from TSDoc into a generated vitest file per atom — positive examples must compile and run green; negative compile-error examples are asserted with @ts-expect-error under tsc; negative Result-error examples execute and assert the declared error. An example that stops compiling fails the atom's check the same run the API changed. This is the estate's validators-must-recompute doctrine applied to documentation, and it makes the ≥-examples rule self-policing against filler (filler that must execute is real code).
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Verified examples give agents a zero-search, zero-debug reuse path and auto-detect doc drift at the change that caused it, which is the cheapest possible moment.

findings.title: Performance budgets: demote from per-atom to complexity-contract atoms; benches prove growth curves within-run, never wall-clock across runs
findings.body: No bench harness exists anywhere in the estate today; safe-path is 56 source lines of string ops and result's combinators are O(1) wrappers — a regression fence on these measures CI-runner noise, and one flaky fence blocking an unrelated PR is a direct innovation slowdown. Even 'relative' fences compare across runs on shared runners, which is still noise. Amend: proportionality key = a declared performance contract. An atom carries benches only when its TSDoc declares an algorithmic-complexity or throughput claim (graph-core canonicalisation, whose rdf-canonize worst case is superpolynomial, is the genuine case); the bench form is within-run ratio measurement (tinybench under vitest bench: candidate vs an in-run baseline op, asserting the declared growth curve across input sizes) — machine-independent, consistent with the frame's own 'machine-independent behaviour' clause, immune to runner variance. Cadence: on package change via declared turbo inputs, never cron. The instrument checks bench presence exactly where a complexity claim exists and rejects benches asserting absolute milliseconds.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: Perf proof lands only where a perf contract exists, so the estate never pays harness maintenance or false-positive fence stalls on O(1) atoms while the one atom that can regress superlinearly is fenced by a noise-immune check.

findings.title: Packed smoke: keep, but as ONE shared instrument with a Windows leg for path-semantics atoms — never ten bespoke scripts
findings.body: Packed smoke is the highest-yield element on the bar for this estate (ESM exports-map and types-resolution defects are exactly what pnpm+tsup packages ship silently), so keep it — but the risk is each atom hand-rolling its own smoke script, the survey-machinery failure mode this node's own dependency (survey-machinery-deconstruction) exists to cure. Amend: a single workspace-config-provided turbo task runs @arethetypeswrong/cli + publint + a minimal import-and-invoke smoke against `pnpm pack` output (none of these tools exist in the repo today — they must be adopted, not reinvented); atoms declare nothing but their entry points. Add a Windows CI leg for the path-semantics atoms (safe-path, workspace-config) — Windows path semantics bit the estate hard this week, and the atom tier is where that defect class multiplies.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: One shared, cache-friendly smoke instrument proves the shipped form of every atom for near-zero marginal cost per atom, and the Windows leg kills the cross-platform defect class at the tier where fixing it is a one-function change.

findings.title: Progressive README per atom: hand-author only non-recomputable sections; API and examples sections are generated or surface-diffed
findings.body: The README's API and examples sections duplicate TSDoc, and no instrument checks README truth — at 10 packages growing toward 30, drift is guaranteed and a stale README misroutes the agent at discovery time. The bar also currently homes examples in three places (TSDoc, README, the frame's standalone 'examples' clause). Amend: TSDoc is the single example source; README hand-authors only what cannot be recomputed — purpose, boundaries, error meaning, removal condition — and its API/examples sections are generated from TSDoc (typedoc-plugin-markdown) or, minimally, the conformance instrument diffs README-listed symbols against the real export surface and fails on mismatch. This is the validators-must-recompute rule applied to the discovery surface.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: A README that cannot drift keeps atom discovery reliable for agents and removes a per-change documentation-sync tax from every future API edit.

findings.title: Atom register: at-bar status must be computed at check time, never a committed column
findings.body: The sketch commits a register whose rows carry a disposition including 'at-bar' — a recorded status the conformance instrument can recompute, which is precisely the recorded-not-recomputed rot the estate's validators-must-recompute rule and the adjacent survey-machinery deconstruction exist to kill. Amend the register schema: rows store only non-recomputable human facts — candidate identity, gate blocker, owner ruling, removal condition, in-waiting rationale; at-bar/not-at-bar is emitted by the conformance instrument at every check run and is never committed. Instrument: the register validator fails any row containing a status field the instrument can recompute. The instrument itself should be one validator in the existing agent-tools CLI (per the use-built-agent-tools-cli rule), not a new package with its own bar-conformance recursion.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: A register that stores only human facts cannot silently lie about conformance, so no future session burns context reconciling a stale status column against reality.

findings.title: Add: a committed, diffed API-surface report per atom — the bar's missing fence against the fan-out killer
findings.body: The candidate bar hardens tests, docs, and perf but leaves unpriced the thing fan-out punishes most: public-surface churn. A high-fan-out atom whose API shifts silently charges every consumer a migration — the exact multiplied cost the programme exists to remove. Instrument: api-extractor (or a ts-morph-generated surface snapshot) emits a committed .api.md per atom; CI diffs it, so any surface change is visible in review and must be classified additive or breaking before merge. This simultaneously implements the sketch's 'validated strict API' clause mechanically — an incidental export IS a report diff — replacing a bespoke strictness checker with an industry instrument the repo does not yet have (no api-extractor, attw, or publint present today). Pairs with the prefix-is-a-wire-field discipline already in doctrine: surface changes become deliberate, versioned events.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: When the atom tier's contracts can only change visibly and deliberately, consumers upgrade cheaply and trust compounds — API stability at high fan-out is the single largest purchasable input to cheap future change.

findings.title: The excellence contract's core clauses (Result totality, structural boundaries, TDD, removal condition) survive the attack
findings.body: For completeness of the adversarial sweep: the contract-and-boundaries clauses (one responsibility, Result<T,E> totality, enforced dependency direction via the existing oak-eslint boundary rules and depcruise, removal condition) and TDD-as-atomic-landing were pressure-tested and hold — each is enforced by an instrument that already exists in the estate, each has a stated link to change-cost, and none imposes per-atom marginal ceremony beyond writing the code correctly once. No change proposed.
findings.innovationSpeedLink: These clauses are the already-paid-for portion of the bar; their instruments exist and their per-atom marginal cost is near zero, so they buy blast-radius reduction without taxing future atoms.
